note:
The name Micah is an abbreviated form of _Micayahu_ (“Who is like Yahweh?”). The town of Moresheth is located near Gath in the Shephelah, or foothills, of southwestern Judah.

**which he saw.** The divine message to Micah takes the form of a supernatural revelation to the prophet’s inner sight or hearing. The verb “saw” is related to the word “vision” (Nah. 1:1).

This prophecy has four parts: summons of the nations to attend the trial (v. 2); a symbolic vision of God overthrowing creation (vv. 3, 4); an accusation against the two capital cities (v. 5); and the divine sentence for Samaria to be destroyed (vv. 6, 7).

**1:2 all of you ... against you.** God’s judgment of Samaria (vv. 6, 7) exemplifies and prefigures His judgment against all people who commit idolatry and social crimes.

**his holy temple.** That is, His heavenly abode (Ps. 11:4).

Behind the march of the Assyrian army, the prophet sees the hand of God (cf. Is. 10:5, 6). The depth of divine judgment against Jerusalem and Samaria is vividly portrayed as a destruction of the created order itself.

**1:3 high places.** Whoever controls Israel’s heights controls the land. This probably refers to such mountains rather than to the Canaanite shrines known as “high places.”
These words link the symbolic vision with the historical overthrow of Samaria (vv. 6, 7), which is located on a hill (1 Kin. 16:24).

“Jacob” and “Israel” often occur together in Micah, referring to the entire covenant people. Sometimes “Jacob” represents the people as a whole (2:12; 3:1, 8, 9). The second occurrence of “Jacob” in this verse points to the northern kingdom of Israel (with its capital, Samaria) as distinct from Judah (with its capital, Jerusalem). In this book “Israel” generally designates Judah as representing the whole nation.

Ancient Near Eastern fertility religions involved ritual prostitution, an activity strictly forbidden to Israel (Deut. 23:17). The wealth that has been paid to the temple prostitutes and used to make idols will be taken by the Assyrians and used in the same way.

This lament has three parts: an introduction stating Micah’s resolve to mourn Judah’s exile (vv. 8, 9); a main body with a series of wordplays on the names of Judah’s stronghold predicting Judah’s fall and exile (vv. 10–15); and a conclusion calling the house of David to join in mourning rites because it will go into exile (v. 16).

**stripped and naked.** A symbolic act referring to the threat of captivity (Is. 20:2–4).
Assyria’s King Sennacherib reached Jerusalem’s gate but did not take the city (v. 12; see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

Micah’s lament over the fall of David’s house recalls David’s lament over the fall of Saul’s house under similar circumstances (2 Sam. 1:20). The Philistine city of Gath should not be given reason to rejoice over the coming calamity.

“Tell” and “Gath” sound alike in Hebrew, and throughout this oracle there are a number of such wordplays on the names of the towns mentioned. They are located in the Shephelah near Micah’s home.

**roll yourselves in the dust.** A vivid expression of grief over a humiliating defeat (Jer. 6:26), incorporating a play on the name Beth-le-aphrah (“House of Dust”), a place of unknown location.

Its location is unknown. The name sounds like a word for “beautiful” and is an ironic wordplay on the fate of its citizens taken into exile.

**Zaanan ... out.** Despite its name, which echoes the Hebrew for “come out,” this town will cower behind its wall and not “come out” to battle.

**Beth-ezel.** Lit. “adjoining house.” The Hb. word _ezel_ resembles a verb meaning “withdraw” or “withhold.” This town will withhold its protection from Judah because it has been annexed by the conqueror.
Though it has longed for good, this town, whose name sounds like “bitterness,” will experience the harshness of defeat.

A major fortress town of Judah located twenty-six miles (42 km) southwest of Jerusalem, Lachish house a contingent of chariots. Here the reference to “steeds” (the Hb. term resembles “Lachish”) perhaps implies that the chariots will be used for flight rather than for fighting.

**the beginning of sin.** The precise nature of this sin is not explained. Many suggest that it involves the import of Egyptian horses for use in war (5:10; Deut. 17:16; 1 Kin. 10:28, 29), inducing Israel to rely on her military strength rather than on the Lord.

**daughter of Zion.** A personification of Jerusalem (Zeph. 3:14 note).

This allusion to the dowry given by a father to his daughter as she departs for her husband’s house (1 Kin. 9:16) is motivated by the similarity of Moresheth to the Hb. term for a “woman who is betrothed.” The inhabitants of Moresheth-gath (the prophet’s hometown, about twenty miles [32 km] southwest of Jerusalem and six miles [10 km] northeast of Lachish) will depart into exile.

**Achzib shall be a deceitful thing.** The town’s name closely resembles the Hb. term for “deceitful,” a word used for the “deceitful brook” in Jer. 15:18. The town of Achzib (nine miles [14km] east of Gath) will disappoint the king of Judah.

The term sounds like Mareshah, another fortress town in the foothills south of Jerusalem, lying five miles (8 km) northeast of Lachish. The “conqueror” undoubtedly refers to Assyria.

**glory of Israel ... Adullam.** As David fled to the wilderness cave at Adullam (2 Sam. 23:13), so the leaders (“glory”) of Israel will flee. The body of the lament (vv. 10–15) begins and ends with literary references to David’s career (v. 10 note).
A culturally recognized sign of bereavement that in normal circumstances is forbidden to Israel (Deut. 14:1).

This prophecy has three parts: (1) the accusation—evil and violent men unethically seize sacred property and destroy its owners (vv. 1, 2); (2) the sentence—the Lord sentences them to exile (v. 3) and loss of their lands to invaders (v. 4); and (3) the conclusion—the robbers are cut off from the covenant people (v. 5). The accusation and sentence are linked by a play on words involving “who devise wickedness” (v. 1) and “I am devising disaster” (v. 3), which are virtually identical expressions in Hebrew. As the powerful have taken fields away from Israel’s families (vv. 1, 2), so the Lord will send an enemy army to wrest the Promised Land from them (vv. 4, 5).

**2:1 in the power of their hand.** They misuse their status to perpetrate oppression.
A family’s property is a permanent, sacred trust from God (Lev. 25:10, 13). See note on Num. 27:1–11.
A reference either to God giving their land to the Assyrians or to the Assyrian conqueror distributing their fields to others as booty.
After the Babylonian exile the land will be redistributed (cf. Num. 26:55; Josh. 18:8–10), but neither the oppressors nor their descendants will then be present to claim an inheritance.

In this prophecy, Micah defends his message against those who seek to silence him. Micah rebuffs their command to cease (v. 6). Then the Lord accuses the powerful of exploiting the defenseless (vv. 8, 9) and sentences them to exile because they have defiled the land (v. 10). Finally, the people are condemned for desiring false prophets who tell them what they want to hear (v. 11).

**2:6** The Hebrew of v. 6 is difficult to translate. Some suggest that Micah confronts false prophets who support the land robbers and who have sought to silence him. In support of this interpretation, the Hb. phrase rendered “thus they preach” (lit. “drip [words]”) can be translated “they prophesy.” Others argue that the greedy and corrupt leaders themselves have tried to silence the prophet.
From this point to the end of the chapter, Micah directly relays the word of the Lord.

The oppressed belong to Israel’s middle class (Introduction: Date and Occasion).

**2:8 with no thought of war.** Expecting peace in their homeland where they feel most secure, Israel’s people are plundered instead.
The people have grown so spiritually inept that they will easily be deceived by a charlatan or false prophet.

Micah concludes the first section of his prophecy with a brief oracle of salvation. Expositors differ as to the particular event primarily in view. Some consider the passage to foreshadow the eventual return from the exile. The Lord will make a breach in the defenses of their captors and lead His flock back from the lands where they have been dispersed to the sheepfold of Jerusalem. Alternatively, the passage may refer to the divine deliverance extended to Jerusalem when Sennacherib overran much of the land in 701 B.C. This interpretation receives significant support from the similarity of language between 2:12, 13 and Isaiah’s prophecy, “Out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant,” which definitely refers to 701 (2 Kin. 19:29–31; Is. 37:30–32). The Lord will gather the people into the city for their preservation. He will then break out of the besieged city to deliver them by decimating the Assyrian army (2 Kin. 18:17–19:37). Either reading of a deliverance of God’s chosen remnant anticipates the greater triumph of the Messiah, the great Shepherd-King (5:2–5).

**2:12 Jacob ... Israel.** The second interpretation above requires these to refer to Judah as representing the whole nation (1:5 note), whereas the first interpretation is not restricted in this way.

**2:13 Their king.** Or, more probably, “their King,” in view of the parallelism with the next line.

The three prophecies of this chapter announce the rejection and punishment of Israel’s incompetent, corrupt leadership. First, the leaders’ treatment of the oppressed people is likened to cannibalism (vv. 1–4). Second, the false prophets who led the people astray are condemned (vv. 5–7) and contrasted with Micah, who prophesies true revelations from God (v. 8). Finally, the corrupt political and religious leaders are condemned and their complacency is castigated (vv. 9–12).

**3:1 And I said.** An editorial addition indicating that Micah edited his own book (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). It marks the start of the second cycle of prophecies in this work (chs. 3–5).

**Jacob ... Israel.** Both terms designate Judah as the covenant people (1:5 note).
Just as the magistrates have refused to hear the cries of the oppressed, so God will refuse to hear their cry in the time of judgment.
These false prophets are opportunists, tailoring their pronouncements of peace and security to the desires of those who feed them. See Jer. 28.
Those who have prophesied falsely will be judged and shamed by God’s silence., 7
Micah is divinely inspired not to lull the people into a false sense of security and divine favor, but to expose their iniquity with insight and boldness.

Possibly to be related to the expansion of Jerusalem to accommodate refugees from the north and to the building projects undertaken during the reign of Hezekiah. The prophet Isaiah also highlights the corruption that exists within the city of Jerusalem during this era (Is. 1:14, 15, 21–23).

This prophecy is given in the days of Hezekiah (Jer. 26:17–19). Hez­ekiah’s repentance and faithfulness (cf. Is. 36–38) mean that the complete fulfillment of Micah’s words in the judgment of Jerusalem is delayed until 586 B.C.

Micah’s prophetic vision shifts from impending judgment in the short term to the “latter days,” when the messianic reign of God is established in Zion. The first part of this oracle (vv. 1–5) is virtually identical to Is. 2:1–5 (see notes there for further comment).

**4:1 the latter days.** (cf. Is. 2:2–4) The expression points to a new epoch, which, though in the hidden future, decisively alters the course of history. Here it refers to the messianic age, consummated in the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21; 22).

**mountain of the house of the LORD.** No longer the abandoned remains of 3:12 but the forerunner of the Lord’s presence with His people, earthly Mount Zion prefigures the heavenly reality to which the church indeed has now come (Heb. 12:22–24). As part of the old covenant, the earthly religious center has been eclipsed by the coming new order (Heb. 8:13).

**as the highest of the mountains.** Pagan gods in Micah’s day also have sacred mountains with temples. By being raised above them, God’s eternal house (here symbolized by the temple on Mount Zion) will be established among the nations as the center of true worship.

See note on v. 1.

**assemble ... gather.** The same verbs as in 2:12, indicating that this prophecy is a development and expansion of what was said earlier.

**and those whom.** Perhaps better translated “even those whom,” a further description of the same group.

Just as God preserved a remnant that survived Sennacherib’s invasion (2:12, 13 note), so also a remnant will survive the later Babylonian exile.

**strong nation.** A prophecy that finds final fulfillment in the church (1 Pet. 2:9, 10).

Jerusalem (i.e., the new Jerusalem; Rev. 21, c.f. Heb. 12:22) will become a fortified tower around which the inhabitants will gather for protection. Isaiah anticipates a similar transformation of Jerusalem (Is. 65:17–25).

This prophecy explains that Israel’s present distress (the “now” of vv. 9, 11) will bring glorious salvation—liberation from the later Babylonian exile (vv. 9, 10) and release from Sennacherib’s siege (vv. 11, 12).

The pain of judgment (exile, loss of king and land) for the remnant must precede the birth of the messianic age that will follow.

**to Babylon.** Micah’s vision goes beyond the immediate Assyrian threat to Judah, and anticipates what happens more than a century later when there is no deliverance for Jerusalem from the Babylonians.

The focus is again on the circumstances of Micah’s own day.

**many nations.** The Assyrian imperial army consists of mercenaries from many nations.

This prophecy also moves from present distress (“now”; v. 1) to the Messiah’s coming and victory (vv. 2–5). See Introduction: Christ in Micah.

**5:1 cheek.** This insult to Israel’s leader signifies that Jerusalem will fall to its Babylonian attackers, and all power to resist will be gone (cf. 2 Kin. 25:4–7).

Contrasts the coming ruler with the current humiliated representative of David’s line in v. 1.

**Bethlehem Ephrathah.** Lit. “house of bread, fruitful.” The previously undistinguished town of David’s birth (1 Sam. 16:1–13), situated five miles (8 km) southwest of Jerusalem. Though the Davidic line of kings would temporarily cease (v. 3), God would yet raise up a ruler from David’s family to reign forever—Jesus Christ Himself (2 Sam. 7:12–17; Matt. 2:6).

**for me.** All occurs to advance the divine plan.

**from ancient days.** This expression can also be translated “from days of eternity.” Indeed, “from of old” is rendered “from everlasting” in Hab. 1:12, where it is applied to God Himself (cf. “eternal God,” Deut. 33:27). Micah has certainly learned that the ruler’s origin long predates His anticipated future coming. A more-than-human figure is involved.

Israel was without a Davidic king from the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. until the coming of Christ.

**she who is in labor.** A reference either to Mary, the mother of Jesus, or to the faithful remnant (see 4:10).

**rest of his brothers.** Thousands of Israelites were converted after Pentecost (Acts 2:41, 47).
The messianic ruler is assigned the LORD’s role (2:12) of caring for the flock.

The ruler as “Prince of Peace” (Is. 9:6; cf. also Zech. 9:10) will provide completely for the well-being and security of His people. It is this aspect of Christ’s mission on which Paul reflects in Eph. 2:14.

**the Assyrian.** After the first line of what is now designated v. 5. Micah switches his focus back to contemporary conditions. Assyria, the besieging nation of v. 1, here represents all enemies opposed to God’s kingdom.

**seven ... eight.** Seven is the number of perfection. There will be a more-than-sufficient supply of leaders to expand Christ’s kingdom.
A reference to an ancient king, whose empire included both Babylon and Assyria (Gen. 10:10, 11).

This oracle has two parts: a prophecy that the remnant will become God’s instrument of life and death (vv. 7, 8), and a petition for God to defeat all His foes (see v. 9 and note). These statements find fulfillment in the church (2 Cor. 2:14–16).

**5:7 delay ... wait for.** As rain proceeds from the divine initiative, so the remnant depends on God to refresh the earth.
This verse is perhaps better translated as a petition for divine victory (“Let your hand be lifted against”). How the Lord accomplishes this victory is described in the following section.

God will cleanse His people (vv. 10–14) and cut off the pagan nations (v. 15). God’s salvation cannot come except by stripping His people of all vain and false military confidence (vv. 10, 11), sorceries (v. 12), and idolatry (v. 13).

God’s vengeance will take place when He reveals His full sovereignty by delivering His people and punishing their guilty oppressors. Only the sovereign Lord Himself has the ultimate right to use force to protect His kingdom, and the exercise of force by an individual or community without divine authorization springs from unbelief (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19–21).

The third cycle of Micah’s oracles (chs. 6, 7) opens with a classic example of the prophetic covenant lawsuit in which the Lord pleads the terms of the covenant against His disobedient people. The message opens with a judgment scene in which the Lord is plaintiff, Micah is His envoy, the mountains are witnesses, and Israel is the accused (vv. 1, 2). God’s own covenant faithfulness is then attested as He first gives Israel opportunity to voice any complaints (v. 3) and then recounts His mighty acts of deliverance (vv. 4, 5). The demand for covenant righteousness is then proclaimed—a righteousness consisting not merely in empty ritual but in heartfelt obedience (vv. 6–8).

**6:1 Arise, plead your case.** The Lord commands Micah, as His representative, to prosecute God’s case against the people. Micah obeys the command (v. 2).

**mountains.** The Lord uses the enduring mountains as witnesses to the covenant mediated by Moses (see Deut. 4:26; 30:19 and note; 31:28; 32:1).
The Lord recognizes them as being in covenant bond with himself.

These verses are framed by references to Egypt (from which Israel was delivered) and Gilgal (where Israel entered the Promised Land, Josh. 4:19). All God’s saving acts during Israel’s formative period are included: the Passover and exodus, guidance by the pillar of fire and cloud, miraculous provision of food and water, the provision of able leaders (“Moses, Aaron, and Miriam”), and victory over enemies. God’s wonderful provision for His people during this period foreshadows the church’s experience with Christ (John 6:33; 1 Cor. 5:7; 10:1–4).

**6:5 remember.** This command means not merely mental recall of past events, but that those events are to be a means of actualizing them in the present. By faith, such knowledge of the past is applied to present situations.

**Shittim to Gilgal.** From the last encampment east of the Jordan (Josh. 3:1) to the first encampment west of that river (Josh. 4:19). What is in view is the miraculous drying up of the Jordan.

Through the rhetorical escalation of sacrifices (“calves ... thousands of rams ... rivers of oil ... my firstborn”), Micah displays the absurdity of Israel’s dependence on empty ritual and sacrifice to earn divine favor. Such reliance shows a profound misunderstanding of God’s grace, for Israel’s salvation from Egypt (and ultimately from sin and death) was free and not earned (vv. 4, 5). Moreover, Israel’s covenant obligations entail social justice and mercy, not mere liturgy (v. 8). See also Amos 5:21–24., 7

Or “prudently.” These three divine requirements cover relationships with others, an individual’s inner attachment to the standards of the covenant, and a lifestyle that gives due acknowledgment to God in every aspect of conduct.

This prophecy consists of an address to Jerusalem (v. 9), an accusation of falsity in business dealings and speech (vv. 10–12), and a judicial sentence of disease and ruin (v. 13–15). The covenantal context is apparent as the punishment reflects the covenant curses specified in the Mosaic law (v. 15; Lev. 26:20; Deut. 28:40, 51). Those who live in rebellion against their covenant king will find every endeavor blighted as He frustrates them from achieving what they want.
The bitter conditions foretold in these verses reflect the futility curses described in Lev. 26:26; Deut. 28:30, 31, 38–40., 15

verse_quote: the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab.
note: Omri and Ahab ruled over the northern kingdom during the ninth century B.C.. Notorious for their wicked deeds, they actively promoted the worship of Baal throughout Israel.

Micah laments that no righteous are found (vv. 1–4), and he bemoans the resulting social and national confusion that is both the result and punishment of their sin (vv. 4–6). Particularly striking is the description of the breakdown of family order. Micah concludes, however, with his confidence that beyond God’s judgment lies salvation (v. 7).

**7:1 I have become ... summer fruit.** In his search for the righteous, Micah compares himself to a vinedresser searching for choice fruit after the best of the season has past.

One characterized by loyalty to the covenant (cf. text note on 6:8).

**no one upright.** This verse explains the allegory of v. 1.

verse_quote: The best of them is like a brier.
note:
As with a person searching for choice fruit but finding only briers and thorns, a righteous person cannot be found.

**watchmen.** A metaphor for the prophets who have announced the coming judgment (Ezek. 3:17; 33:7).

This passage is later used in Jewish extrabiblical apocalyptic literature to describe the conflict that will accompany the final day of the Lord. Jesus quotes v. 6 in describing the conflict associated with His coming (Matt. 10:35–39; Luke 12:51–53)., 6

This concluding hymn consists of four stanzas: (1) Lady Jerusalem in her fallen status confesses her sin and her faith in the Lord (vv. 8–10); (2) the prophet promises that she will become a sheepfold offering salvation to the world under judgment (vv. 11–13); (3) Micah prays that the Lord will again miraculously shepherd His people (v. 14), which the Lord promises to do (v. 15), and Micah then prophesies that the unbelieving enemy will be conquered (vv. 16, 17); and (4) the people celebrate God’s forgiveness and faithfulness with a hymn of praise (vv. 18–20).

**7:8 darkness.** A dungeon without light is an apt figure for a city under divine judgment.

verse_quote: I shall look upon his vindication.
note: The Lord’s righteousness will be manifested in faithful Israel’s salvation (vv. 8, 9) and her unbelieving enemy’s destruction (v. 10).

See 4:1, 6; 5:10–15. The last day is symbolically depicted by the restoration of Jerusalem’s city walls (v. 11) and the extension of the boundaries of the land to limits prophesied by Moses and enjoyed under David and Solomon (v. 12; Gen. 15:18; Ex. 23:31; Deut. 11:24; 1 Kin. 4:21, 25).
The Euphrates.
Outside the elect’s secure borders is universal judgment. The last judgment is ultimately in view.
Fertile areas east of the Jordan renowned for their cattle and sheep.

verse_quote: hands on their mouths ... be deaf.
note: These are signs of humiliation in the face of overwhelming divine power. They will no longer taunt Israel or listen to the vain boasts of others.

verse_quote: Who is a God like you.
note:
Micah, whose name means “who is like the Lord?” (1:1 note), perhaps employs a wordplay on his own name to emphasize God’s pardoning grace.

**because he delights in steadfast love.** The word used here (and in v. 20) for “steadfast love” is the familiar Hb. term _hesed._ It refers to God’s utter commitment to the covenant relationship that He sovereignly instituted and that persists despite the waywardness of His covenant partners. He delights to display His resolute and effective commitment by securing pardon and acceptance for them—no matter the cost or difficulty involved. He will thus ensure that the relationship disrupted by their sin will be consummated in accordance with His purpose.
As God began Israel’s journey by casting the Egyptians into the Red Sea (v. 15; cf. Ex. 15:1–5), He will conclude her history by casting His people’s iniquities into the depths.
God’s loving fidelity to the patriarchs is the basis of the church’s hope (Rom. 4:17; Gal. 3:7–9, 29).
